findings.title: Content standards are being pulled into central functions
findings.dataStatement: Several roles in the dataset describe content standards owned by one central or horizontal function, with product teams consuming them rather than setting them. Netflix calls it a “centralized authority” over “a decentralized content design community.” Ally’s Content Architect “sits above channels and formats.” LinkedIn asks for a “single accountable owner.” Adobe draws the line explicitly: the role covers “how terminology, patterns, and guidance are modeled,” not “product-level content decisions or UI copy — that lives with embedded product and domain content teams.”
findings.interpretation: This looks like the design-systems teams of a decade ago: a small central group owns the primitives, and product teams consume them. The embedded model isn’t gone — some roles in this dataset still hire directly onto product teams — but for the most senior systems work, it’s no longer the default path.

findings.title: AI fluency is a baseline, not a differentiator
findings.dataStatement: Several roles in the dataset expect a candidate to already be working with AI tools, not simply curious about them. HelloFresh names the tools directly: “Active usage of AI as a core part of your daily workflow… building rapid interactive prototypes (using tools like Claude Code, Gemini, or Figma AI).” Wealthsimple asks for “shipping your own code changes.” The expectation isn’t limited to AI-native employers — it shows up at a carmaker (GM) and a meal-kit company (HelloFresh) alongside the AI companies you’d expect.
findings.interpretation: Two years ago this would have read as a differentiator. Now it reads the way “proficiency in Figma” reads — stated in the qualifications, not floated as a nice-to-have. Whether an employer builds AI products doesn’t predict whether its content team is expected to use it. What predicts it is whether the content function has been handed a systems mandate, which shows up in whether the responsibilities describe building mechanisms or producing pages.

findings.title: Nobody agrees what this work is worth
findings.dataStatement: Insurify states $65,000 for its “Editor, AI Content Systems” role. Netflix states up to $710,000 for its “Staff Systems Designer, Language” role. Both titles carry the word “Systems.” The numbers aren’t measuring the same thing, either: Netflix says its range is the entire package — “our compensation structure consists solely of an annual salary; we do not have bonuses. You choose each year how much of your compensation you want in salary versus stock options” — while Zoom labels its range “Salary Range or On Target Earnings” and HelloFresh calls its simply “Pay Range,” neither saying which. Extras compound this unevenly: Airbnb’s London posting states its base range “may also be eligible for bonus, equity, benefits, and Employee Travel Credits” — the same language you’d expect from a US posting — while Wise’s and the UK Government Digital Service’s postings name no such extras at all.
findings.interpretation: An order of magnitude between two roles whose titles would sit side by side in a search result isn’t a seniority gap — it’s an absence of consensus about what the discipline actually is. Titles aren’t carrying reliable scope information, and the numbers don’t rescue them: a stated range can mean fixed salary, the whole package, or something the posting never specifies, and nothing about a company’s other choices — US or UK, insurer or travel platform — predicts which. Airbnb’s UK posting carries the same bonus-and-equity language you’d expect from a US tech company; Wise’s doesn’t. A number on its own tells you less about what a candidate can actually expect to take home than it looks like it does.

findings.title: From producing content to producing systems
findings.dataStatement: Several postings say outright that writing is not the job. CoLab says “not by writing content yourself, but by building AI-powered systems.” Ally writes “focused less on creating content and more on making content work.” Adobe's role covers how terminology, patterns, and guidance are modeled, but its stated responsibilities include no product writing at all.
findings.interpretation: This isn’t surprising given the rise of systems work and the steady consolidation of content design teams. Design orgs are shrinking, and content practitioners are stretched across more domains to cover the gap. The lasting impact here is a shift in mindset. Writing, as a prerequisite craft, is no longer a requirement. The real question is whether content designers will embrace that change, and find the same joy in building that they found in writing.

findings.title: Content roles are appearing outside design orgs
findings.dataStatement: Several postings place the role outside a design org entirely, and the placements don't cluster into one alternative either. HelloFresh files its Staff AI Content Designer under “Category: Software Engineering.” Ally's Content Architect sits in “Career area: Marketing.” Notion's is in Customer Experience; LinkedIn's in a Knowledge Management Solutions team under a department it calls GBO. Adobe tags its role to two categories at once — Design, and Engineering and Product. CoLab, Insurify, The Ride Platform, and Meta's AI Content Strategy Lead (in Business Marketing) all sit in marketing or editorial functions while their stated responsibilities describe systems work, not campaign or editorial production.
findings.interpretation: The discipline is being claimed by several functions at once, and none of them has won. The conversation about content design's future tends to assume it stays inside design — these postings don't.
